clue.text: Malleable adhesive as once used to seal cracked ebony?

indicators.note: to seal something is to close it inside, so one piece is shut within the other

parts.note: ebony is the colour black; 'cracked' shows it opened up to take a filling
ut is Latin for 'as', an old word now out of use

explanation.surface: A tip on mending split ebony with a pliable glue, the way it used to be done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cracked' shows the colour word opened up to take a filling. Blu-Tack is the brand name of the putty-like reusable adhesive.
explanation.definitionFit: Blu-Tack is a soft, pliable putty sold for sticking posters to walls, a trade name used generically.

clue.text: Bum ref is wrong about Hearts — his specs are dodgy! (12, two words)

parts.note: bum and bottom both mean the backside

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go round the next piece
wrong letters are out of place, so they must be put into a different order

parts.note: the letters of these words
H is the card-game abbreviation for hearts

explanation.surface: A football fan's rant at a referee about a Hearts game: his glasses must be faulty.
explanation.walkthrough: Hearts is also an Edinburgh football club. 'specs' looks like spectacles but means speculations: a bottom fisher buys shares that have crashed in value.
explanation.definitionFit: A bottom fisher is an investor who buys distressed or very cheap stocks, risky speculative purchases.

clue.text: Gaudy bird heading off for mountain region to the north

indicators.note: in a down entry, going north means reading upward, from the bottom back to the top
the heading is what comes first, and taking it off removes the opening letter

parts.note: the Tyrol is an Alpine region of Austria and Italy

explanation.surface: A bright-plumaged bird setting off northward for the Alps.
explanation.definitionFit: A lory is a small brightly coloured parrot of Australasia, so gaudy describes its plumage well.

clue.text: Seen this Indian tourist destination? For 'Indus a rupee, that's fantastic

indicators.note: fantastic means fanciful, so the letters are freely reimagined in a new order
For says the quoted phrase stands for two things together, so one of them must be taken back out

parts.note: the letters of the quoted phrase
taken as written; these letters are removed from the rearranged phrase

explanation.surface: A tourist asks whether you have visited, quoting a garbled boast about a river and a coin.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: 'For' means the quoted letters stand in for SEEN plus the answer, so take SEEN away from them and arrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Udaipur, the City of Lakes in Rajasthan, is a famous destination for visitors to India.

clue.text: Theatre award for old Gaby Smart

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the American prize for Broadway theatre
second meaning: an obsolete word for a simpleton, a gaby being a fool

explanation.surface: A stage prize won by an actor named Gaby Smart, now getting on.
explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings, not two: 'Gaby Smart' reads as a person's name, but gaby is a dialect word for a fool, and Smart is a separate meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tony is Broadway's award; tony was once slang for a simpleton; and tony also means classy or upmarket.

clue.text: Cold tailless chicken Jock's fried well?

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
rumpy is a name for a fowl or cat born without a tail

explanation.surface: Leftover chicken, served cold, that a Scot would rather have fried properly.
explanation.walkthrough: Jock is a nickname for a Scot, so the definition wants a Scots word: food fried well is crisp.
explanation.definitionFit: Crumpy is a Scots word meaning crisp or crunchy, which is how well-fried food turns out.

clue.text: Shirt suitable for an Arab sandbank, with an S

parts.note: a kame is a ridge of sand and gravel left by a glacier
es is the spelt-out name of the letter S

explanation.surface: A garment fit for desert life, worn on a sandbank, with a size label.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' just joins the pieces; the spelling of the letter's name supplies the last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The kamees or kameez is a long loose tunic worn in South Asia and the Arab world, from Arabic qamis, a shirt.

clue.text: Marks absorbed by sudden thrusts in leg armour

indicators.note: something absorbed is taken inside another thing, so the first piece goes within the second

parts.note: a jab is a quick sudden thrust or punch
M is the abbreviation for the old German currency, marks

explanation.surface: Scratches made by quick stabs at a knight's leg armour.
explanation.walkthrough: M goes inside JABS, after the second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Jambs (or jambes) are pieces of medieval armour protecting the lower leg, from French jambe.

clue.text: Potentially beneficial fluids, artesian in origin

indicators.note: something in its origin is in the raw form it came from, so the true word is a rearrangement of it

parts.note: the letters of this word

explanation.surface: Health-giving waters that come up from an artesian well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'artesian' sets up spring water, but it is only the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Antisera are blood serums rich in antibodies, given to treat or protect against disease.

clue.text: I'm AZ, fussed about rule — official

indicators.note: about means around, so the jumbled letters wrap the next piece
to be fussed is to be flustered and agitated, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters of these words, apostrophe dropped
R is the abbreviation for rule

explanation.surface: Azed himself, flustered about a regulation, owns up as the authority.
explanation.walkthrough: AZ is a nod to the setter Azed; here it is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Mirza is a Persian title of honour once used for princes and also given to officials and secretaries.

clue.text: Room for prisoners once in court — beer departs in beer mug

definitions.text: Room for prisoners once in court

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces inside the word for the drinking vessel

parts.note: a bock is a large glass or mug for beer
ale is a kind of beer
D is the timetable abbreviation for departs

explanation.surface: A cell for prisoners in old courtrooms, then someone draining a pint glass.
explanation.walkthrough: D is the timetable abbreviation, as on a departures board. The Old Bailey is London's central criminal court.
explanation.definitionFit: The bale-dock or bail-dock was a small room at the old Old Bailey where prisoners waited to be tried.

clue.text: Backstage worker excited by finest cheers

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up and restless, so the letters are moved around

parts.note: the letters of these words

explanation.surface: A stagehand thrilled by the loudest applause of the night.
explanation.definitionFit: A sceneshifter moves stage scenery between scenes, working out of sight of the audience.

clue.text: Super-intellectual providing support on the spot with first clue?

parts.note: a bra is a supporting undergarment
in means present, at the place
the first clue of a crossword is 1 Across, written 1AC

explanation.surface: A genius tutor offers on-the-spot help with the opening clue of the puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the self-referential trick: 'first clue' is read as its label, 1 Across, with 1 taken as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A brainiac is slang for an exceptionally clever person, a super-intellectual.

clue.text: Copy of legal document a PR mustn't get damaged

indicators.note: damaged letters have been knocked out of shape, so they must be rearranged

parts.note: the letters of these words, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A warning that a public-relations person must not spoil an important legal paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A transumpt is an archaic legal term for an exact copy or transcript of a record.

clue.text: Change in e.g. Kazakhstan leaders for this year, incredibly young and new

indicators.note: leaders are the ones at the front, so take the opening letter of each following word

parts.words: this year, incredibly young and new
parts.note: initials of this, year, incredibly, young and new; 'and' is skipped

explanation.surface: A remark that Kazakhstan's rulers this year are remarkably young and fresh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' is small change, coins: the tyiyn is the hundredth part of the Kazakh tenge.
explanation.definitionFit: The tyiyn is a small coin of Kazakhstan and nearby states, the loose change of their currency.

clue.text: Caribbean form of Buddhism (old) withered

parts.note: WI stands for the West Indies
Zen is a school of Buddhism

explanation.surface: An old Caribbean strain of Buddhism that has dried up.
explanation.walkthrough: '(old)' flags that wizen as an adjective is an archaic form of wizened.
explanation.definitionFit: Wizen, an old adjective now replaced by wizened, describes something shrivelled and dried up.

clue.text: Old Baron engaged in favourite pursuit, having friendly chats

indicators.note: engaged in means occupied within something, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: a hobby is a favourite pastime
nob is dated slang for a nobleman or toff

explanation.surface: An old aristocrat at his favourite pastime, chatting away amiably.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' flags that nob is dated slang; the baron is not a B here.
explanation.definitionFit: Hobnobby is an adjective from hobnob, to socialise familiarly, so it describes people chatting on easy terms.

clue.text: Famous bender with piles scattered around in old-style superfluity

indicators.note: around means enclosing, so the rearranged letters surround the first piece
scattered things are spread out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of this word
Uri Geller is famous for bending spoons

explanation.surface: A celebrated drunkard surrounded by heaps of excess, in an old-fashioned setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bender' suggests a drinking spree, but it is the spoon-bending showman.
explanation.definitionFit: Plurisie is an obsolete spelling of plurisy, Shakespeare's word for a superabundance or excess.

clue.text: Old appendage to lance I put by grave in haste, tip missing

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces inside the following word
the tip is an end, and missing means it is gone, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: speed is haste
taken as written
grave and sad both mean serious, solemn

explanation.surface: A soldier hastily puts a knightly attachment for his lance beside a grave.
explanation.walkthrough: The appendage is to the word lance, not the weapon: lancespeisade was an old name for a lance corporal, the lowest rank of officer.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic rank lancespeisade or lancepesade, a lance corporal, puts this ending after lance.

clue.text: Well, I never will imbibe vintage Scotch with must

indicators.note: to imbibe is to drink in, so one piece swallows the other

parts.note: 'my!' is an exclamation of surprise
ould is a Scots and Irish spelling of old

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise at someone mixing old whisky with grape juice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Must' looks like grape juice for wine-making, but here it is mould or mustiness.
explanation.definitionFit: Must is an old word for mould or mustiness, so something with must is mouldy.

clue.text: One making squiggly notes?

parts.note: surface reading: a doodler or a careless writer of messages
setter's reading: shorthand outlines are squiggles taken down as notes

explanation.walkthrough: Shorthand writing looks like squiggles, so the person taking dictation in it fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A steno, short for stenographer, takes down speech in shorthand, whose symbols are curved strokes.

clue.text: Cutting part of bible an ancient misguided church council could be so described

definitions.text: church council could be so described

indicators.note: misguided means led astray, so the letters go off in a different order
cutting something out removes it, so those letters are dropped from the phrase

parts.note: NT is the New Testament, part of the Bible
the letters of these words

explanation.surface: Censoring scripture is what some wayward early synod might be accused of.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove NT from the phrase, then rearrange the remaining seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicaean means of Nicaea, where two ecumenical church councils met in 325 and 787.

clue.text: Shock, being born a weakling?

parts.note: b. is the abbreviation for born
the runt is the weakest of a litter

explanation.surface: Dismay at a baby arriving small and frail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being' only joins the pieces in the surface; the definition is the noun shock, the main force of an impact.
explanation.definitionFit: The brunt is the main impact or shock of a blow or attack, as in bearing the brunt.

clue.text: Retinal layers see you right round soft back of eye

indicators.note: right round means going completely about, so one piece encloses the others

parts.note: ta-ta is a casual goodbye, like see you
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, soft

indicators.note: 'back of' keeps only the first letter of 'eye'

parts.note: the last letter of eye

explanation.surface: An eye doctor's farewell after looking round the back of the eye at its layers.
explanation.walkthrough: P and E sit in the middle of TATA. 'back of eye' sounds anatomical, apt beside retinal, but means its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tapeta, plural of tapetum, are reflective layers behind the retina in many animals' eyes.

clue.text: Night flyer of old? O, this is one that can't fly

parts.words: O, this is one that can't fly
parts.note: O plus this answer makes a famously flightless bird

explanation.surface: An old tale of a nocturnal bird, then a cry that it is grounded.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'O, this' as the letter O followed by the answer: together they make the flightless bird, so the answer is that bird with its O removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Strich is an obsolete word for the screech owl, from Latin strix, a bird that flies by night.

clue.text: Irish stream, not in Leinster, meandering

indicators.note: a meandering course winds about, so the letters wander into a new order
not in tells you the two letters spelling in must be taken away

parts.note: Leinster is the eastern province of Ireland

explanation.surface: A river winding across Ireland that somehow skirts the province of Leinster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irish stream' looks like a noun for a river, but it is a verb: to trail or stream along.
explanation.definitionFit: Streel is an Irish verb meaning to trail or stream along, or wander aimlessly.

clue.text: Never made earlier, it's time for start of surge in profit

indicators.note: one thing being put for another means a swap, here a letter for time replacing another

parts.note: an increase is a gain or profit
T is the abbreviation for time

indicators.note: 'start of' keeps only the first letter of 'surge'

parts.note: the first letter of surge

explanation.surface: A boast that a surge in profit has never been seen before.
explanation.walkthrough: The S in the word for profit is swapped for T. 'earlier' tells you the definition is an old word.
explanation.definitionFit: Increate is an archaic word for uncreated, existing without having been made, as said of God.

clue.text: What chronicler keeps pens?

indicators.note: keeps means holds within, so the letters are held inside the words

parts.note: the end of chronicler joined to the first letter of keeps

explanation.surface: A puzzle over which writing tools a historian keeps on the desk.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a clerk is someone who pens records, much as a chronicler does.
explanation.definitionFit: A clerk is an office worker who keeps records and accounts, writing them out by hand.

clue.text: Institute cutting pay no longer wealthy

indicators.note: something cutting into another thing goes inside it

parts.note: sold is an obsolete word for pay or wages, the root of soldier
I is the abbreviation for Institute

explanation.surface: A body whose pay cuts have left its staff poorer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no longer wealthy' looks like ruin, but it marks an obsolete sense: solid once meant financially substantial.
explanation.definitionFit: Solid formerly meant well-off and financially substantial, a sense now out of use, hence no longer.

clue.text: What Scotch terriers do — a feature of many affenpinschers too

indicators.note: a feature is part of something, so the letters are found inside the following words

parts.note: the end of many joined to the start of affenpinschers

explanation.surface: Scottish terriers and affenpinschers, a small German toy breed, share a habit.
explanation.definitionFit: Nyaff is a Scots verb meaning to yelp or yap like a small dog, which terriers in Scotland would do.

clue.text: You no longer will get to pouch sitter? It was the devilish spirit!

indicators.note: to pouch something is to put it in a bag, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: ye is the archaic word for you
an MP is the sitting member for a constituency

explanation.surface: An accusation that a demon made you grab a sitting duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It was' marks an obsolete spelling: ympe is an old form of imp.
explanation.definitionFit: Ympe is an obsolete spelling of imp, a small devil or mischievous sprite.

clue.text: A type of folk song

parts.note: surface reading: a broad category of traditional music
setter's reading: one particular national folk form, the Portuguese one

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is almost a plain definition; I found no hidden wordplay, so treat it as a deadpan description of one specific genre.
explanation.definitionFit: Fado is the melancholy traditional song style of Portugal, especially Lisbon and Coimbra.

clue.text: Fudge or butterscotch? We tucked in to taste 'em merrily

indicators.note: something tucked in is pushed inside, so one piece goes among the others
doing something merrily is doing it in a giddy, carefree way, so the letters tumble about

parts.note: the letters of these words, apostrophe dropped
taken as written; 'tucked in' puts it among the other letters

explanation.surface: Offering a choice of sweets, then everyone digging in happily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucked in' looks like eating, but it places WE among the other letters before the shake-up. The question mark admits the definition is by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Fudge and butterscotch are both examples of a sweetmeat, an old word for a sugary confection.

clue.text: Bacchian Abderite, confused

indicators.note: confused letters are muddled up, so they need sorting into a new order

parts.note: the letters of this word

explanation.surface: A citizen of Abdera, home of Democritus, befuddled by wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacchian relates to Bacchus, god of wine, hence drunken; ebriated is an old word for intoxicated.

clue.text: Passes for Glasgow Ranger's header certainly catching edge of woodwork

indicators.note: a header is the top or first part, so take the opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of Ranger

indicators.note: catching something means holding it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: yes means certainly

indicators.note: an edge is an extremity, here the final letter of the word that follows

parts.note: the last letter of woodwork

explanation.surface: A Rangers striker's header surely hits the post, on a football pitch in Glasgow.
explanation.walkthrough: Rangers is a Glasgow football club. K goes inside YES, after R. 'for Glasgow' marks a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ryke is a Scots verb meaning to reach or hand over, so it can stand for passes in Scotland.

clue.text: One transfers property, a legal right alternatively

parts.note: taken as written
a lien is a legal right to hold property until a debt is paid
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A conveyancer, or a lien held against an estate as another option.
explanation.definitionFit: In law an alienor is the party who alienates, conveying title in property to another person.
